lead: Metal cutting turns a layer of material into a chip by intense shear. The cutting edge pushes into the work, the material ahead compresses, then slides along a narrow shear plane. Orthogonal cutting is the simple two-dimensional case: the edge is perpendicular to the cutting velocity. Oblique cutting is the three-dimensional case: the edge is tilted by an inclination angle, so the chip flows sideways. Shops use these models to choose rake angle, feed and speed, predict chip thickness and explain surface finish on lathes, milling cutters and drills.
prereq: You need plastic deformation and shear from Unit 2, Bulk Metal Forming Processes.

blocks.text: Orthogonal cutting is the simplest model of machining. The cutting edge is a straight line perpendicular to the cutting velocity. The tool removes a rectangular layer of work material. The model has two dimensions: the cutting direction and the chip thickness direction. It ignores edge tilt and sideways chip flow, so it is a teaching and test model, not a full shop model.

items: Cutting speed v (m/min) is the relative speed between tool and workpiece.
Feed f (mm/rev) is the tool advance per revolution; in turning it sets the uncut chip thickness in many orthogonal tests.

Depth of cut d (mm) is the thickness of the layer removed in one pass. In orthogonal tests d is the uncut chip thickness t₁; the width of cut b (mm), measured along the cutting edge, is the other dimension (b equals the feed in orthogonal tube turning).
Uncut chip thickness t₁ (mm) is the layer thickness ahead of the cutting edge.
Chip thickness t₂ (mm) is the thickness of the chip after it has sheared and left the edge.
Rake angle α (degrees) is the angle between the rake face and a plane perpendicular to the cutting velocity.
Shear angle φ (degrees) is the angle between the shear plane and the cutting velocity.

sections.h3: Chip formation and the shear plane

blocks.text: The tool does not split the metal like a knife. It compresses a small zone ahead of the edge. The metal first deforms elastically. It then yields and shears plastically along a narrow band called the shear plane. Most of the work of cutting becomes heat in this band.

items: Tool engages: the edge contacts the uncut layer of thickness t₁.
Compression: the layer ahead of the edge is squeezed; elastic strain becomes plastic strain.
Shear plane: intense shear starts on a narrow plane at angle φ to the cutting velocity.
Chip slides: the sheared metal moves up the rake face; it is thicker, t₂ > t₁.
Chip leaves: the chip curls away as continuous, discontinuous, built-up edge or segmented form.

blocks.where: r is the chip thickness ratio (no unit); t₁ is uncut chip thickness (mm); t₂ is chip thickness (mm). Since t₂ > t₁, r is less than 1.

blocks.text: tan φ = (r cos α) / (1 − r sin α)
blocks.where: φ is the shear angle (degrees); r is the chip thickness ratio; α is the rake angle (degrees). Use degrees consistently in the trigonometric functions.

blocks.text: This relation is the standard orthogonal model. A larger rake angle α raises φ for the same r, so the shear plane becomes steeper. With t₁ fixed, a larger α raises r and the chip leaves thinner. Forces on the shear plane are resolved in Merchant's circle.

sections.h3: Chip types, built-up edge and oblique cutting

blocks.text: Chip type is set by work material, cutting speed, feed, rake angle, friction and coolant. The four standard types are:

items: Continuous chip: ductile work, high speed, large rake and low friction. The chip is a long ribbon, finish is good, but it can tangle; a chip breaker is used.
Discontinuous chip: brittle work or low speed with high friction. The chip breaks into short pieces; finish is fair and the tool sees impact loads.
Continuous chip with built-up edge (BUE): work material welds to the edge, grows, then breaks away. It gives a rough surface and fragments; it can protect the edge but raises friction.
Segmented chip: shear localises in bands, making a saw-tooth chip. It appears in hard alloys such as titanium and nickel alloys at some speeds.

blocks.text: Built-up edge changes the effective rake angle and the depth of cut. It is unstable, so the surface finish varies along the work. A clean continuous chip with a chip breaker usually gives the best finish.

Oblique cutting is the three-dimensional case. The cutting edge is inclined at angle i to the plane normal to the cutting velocity. The chip does not flow perpendicular to the edge; it flows at a chip flow angle. The effective rake measured in the chip flow direction differs from the normal rake angle. Only a few universities teach the full oblique geometry; most exams ask the definition, the inclination angle and the effect on chip flow.

examples.question: Orthogonal turning of a mild steel tube gives uncut chip thickness t₁ = 0.25 mm and chip thickness t₂ = 0.60 mm. The rake angle is α = 10°. Find the chip thickness ratio r and the shear angle φ.
steps: Chip thickness ratio: r = t₁ / t₂ = 0.25 / 0.60 = 0.4167.
Convert rake angle to radians for the trigonometric terms: α = 10° = 0.1745 rad.
examples.check:
import math
t1 = 0.25
t2 = 0.60
alpha = math.radians(10)
r = t1 / t2
tanphi = (r * math.cos(alpha)) / (1 - r * math.sin(alpha))
phi = math.degrees(math.atan(tanphi))
print('{:.4f}'.format(r))
print('{:.2f}'.format(phi))

traps: Using r = t₂/t₁. The definition is r = t₁/t₂, so r is less than 1 for a normal chip.
Putting degrees into sin and cos on a calculator set to radians, or getting tan φ in radians and reporting it as degrees.

In oblique cutting, state the rake you mean: the normal rake αn is measured in the normal plane, while the effective rake is measured in the chip flow direction. Do not mix the inclination angle i with the chip flow angle.
Saying a continuous chip is always good. A long continuous chip can tangle; a chip breaker is needed, and a BUE chip is continuous but gives poor finish.
Confusing feed f (mm/rev), depth of cut d (mm) and uncut chip thickness t₁ (mm). They have different units and different roles.

quiz.q: Define uncut chip thickness t₁ and chip thickness t₂ in orthogonal cutting.
quiz.a: t₁ is the thickness of the layer ahead of the cutting edge; t₂ is the chip thickness after shear.

quiz.q: Why is the chip thicker than the uncut layer in orthogonal cutting?
quiz.a: The tool compresses and shears the layer along the shear plane. The chip leaves with a lower velocity component along the rake face, so the same volume of metal occupies a shorter length and a larger thickness; t₂ > t₁.

quiz.q: In orthogonal cutting, t₁ = 0.20 mm, t₂ = 0.50 mm and α = 0°. Find r and φ.
A continuous chip with a built-up edge gives poor surface finish. Explain why the finish varies along the cut.
quiz.a: BUE grows and breaks away repeatedly. While it is present it changes the effective edge shape and depth; when it breaks, fragments mark the surface. The cycle repeats, so roughness changes along the work.

quiz.q: State the main difference between orthogonal and oblique cutting.
quiz.a: In orthogonal cutting the cutting edge is perpendicular to the cutting velocity; in oblique cutting the edge is inclined at angle i, so the chip flows sideways and the geometry is three-dimensional.

quiz.q: For r = 0.50 and α = 15°, find the shear angle φ.
Name the four standard chip types.
quiz.a: Continuous, discontinuous, continuous with built-up edge, and segmented.

quiz.q: Why do segmented chips form in some hard alloys?
quiz.a: Shear becomes unstable and localises in narrow bands. The chip has hard, less deformed segments separated by cracks or intense shear bands, giving a saw-tooth shape. This can cause load fluctuations.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry uses finite element models of the shear zone to choose coatings and edge geometry for hard-to-cut alloys. High-speed machining and minimum-quantity lubrication depend on chip flow and segmented chip prediction. Search for 'shear plane model', 'chip flow angle oblique cutting' and 'segmented chip formation titanium' to go further.
